"The biggest governance failures rarely begin with fraud. They often begin with a 'perfectly justified' Related Party Transaction."

As an Independent Director, one question should always come before every Related Party Transaction (RPT):

"Would I approve this transaction if the counterparty were completely unrelated?"

If the answer is No, the discussion should end there.

The reality is that many Related Party Transactions are commercially sensible. They can create operational efficiencies, reduce costs, optimise resources and strengthen business continuity.

The danger begins when commercial convenience overrides fiduciary responsibility.

Under SEBI (LODR) Regulation 23, listed entities must obtain prior Audit Committee approval for RPTs, while material RPTs require shareholder approval, with related parties abstaining from voting. Enhanced disclosures before approval ensure informed decision-making and greater transparency.

As Independent Directors, we should support an RPT only when:
 ✔ It serves the company's interest, not merely the promoter's.
 ✔ Pricing is demonstrably at arm's length.
 ✔ An independent valuation or benchmarking supports the transaction.
 ✔ The commercial rationale is compelling and well documented.
 ✔ Minority shareholders receive fair and equitable treatment.

We should oppose an RPT when:
 ❌ Transparency is compromised.
 ❌ Information is incomplete or selectively presented.
 ❌ Independent valuation is absent where warranted.
 ❌ The transaction transfers value to related parties at the expense of minority shareholders.
 ❌ The governance risk outweighs the commercial benefit.

Consider two Boardrooms:

Board A: A group company supplies specialised components at independently benchmarked market prices. The Audit Committee rigorously challenges management, seeks external validation, and ensures comprehensive disclosures. The transaction creates value for all shareholders.

Board B: A promoter-controlled entity acquires a valuable business asset at an unusually favourable price. Management calls it "strategic" but cannot justify the valuation. Directors approve it without sufficient challenge. Months later, regulatory scrutiny begins—and so do questions about Board independence.

The difference isn't the transaction.
The difference is the Board.

Independent Directors are appointed to protect trust, uphold governance, and preserve shareholder confidence.

In every Related Party Transaction, the real asset at risk is not money - it is the Board's credibility.

Question for Board Members:
What is the single most important question every Independent Director should ask before approving an RPT?

The "Silent Exit" Crisis: Why Independent Directors walk away instead of dissenting.
 
Over 500 mid-term resignations of Independent Directors were recorded across listed companies in India in recent months according to Prime Database & NSE/BSE filings. 
 
While boilerplate SEBI LODR filings routinely cite "preoccupation with other commitments" or "personal reasons", boardroom realpolitik tells a different story. 
 
From PTC India Financial Services (where 3 IDs resigned simultaneously over governance concerns) to VIP Industries, Dhanlaxmi Bank, and Paytm Payments Bank, high-profile exits highlight a growing systemic gap in corporate governance. 

Under the Companies Act, 2013 & SEBI regulations, an ID on the Audit Committee or Nomination & Remuneration Committee (NRC) is expected to act as a guardian of minority shareholder interests.

Yet, when red flags appear whether in Related Party Transactions (RPTs), promoter fund diversions, or capital allocation many experienced IDs opt for a silent resignation rather than a formal note of dissent. 

Why does this happen?

1.    Severe Information Asymmetry: Audit Committees are often rationed quarterly board packs 48 hours in advance, leaving directors as functional "bystanders" to decisions executed weeks prior.

2.    Disproportionate Legal & Personal Liability: Under SEBI, MCA, and regulatory enforcement, IDs face immense personal risk if financial misstatements occur on their watch even when underlying operational data was masked.

3.    Friction in Formal Dissent: Recording a formal dissent note on SEBI LODR filings is high-friction. Without collective board backing, an ID asking uncomfortable questions faces isolation rather than resolution.

The Strategic Takeaway:

For CEOs & Board Chairs: A sudden or quiet ID exit is rarely a calendar issue. It is an information or culture failure.

For Merchant Bankers & Pre-IPO Founders: Appointing domain experts or high-profile names to satisfy compliance means nothing if the boardroom infrastructure restricts raw governance telemetry.

For Executive Search & Recruiters: Board effectiveness is not just about domain talent; it requires evaluating whether management actually welcomes constructive challenge.
 
When regulatory pressure turns Independent Directors into silent exiles rather than accountable watchdogs, institutional memory and investor value both suffer. 

How can Indian boardrooms transition from token compliance to an operational culture where dissent is treated as risk management, not defiance?
Let's discuss here.

post_text:
IPO Ready ≠ Governance Ready

A company may have:
✔️ Strong financial numbers
 ✔️ A reputed merchant banker
 ✔️ An experienced Board
 ✔️ A well-prepared DRHP
 ✔️ All the required policies

But is it really Governance Ready?

This is a question worth asking before the IPO - not after the listing.
Because governance is not just about having the right policies or ticking the compliance boxes.

It is about what happens when the difficult questions are asked.

For example:
• Does the Board genuinely challenge management?
• Does the Audit Committee ask uncomfortable questions - or simply review what is placed before it?
• Are Related Party Transactions only legally compliant, or are they also clearly in the best interest of the company?
• Are whistle-blower concerns reaching the right level?
• Are frequent exits of senior executives, auditors or Independent Directors being treated as warning signals?
• Does the Board receive bad news early - or only after it becomes impossible to ignore?
• Is the company culture ready for the transparency and scrutiny that comes with being a listed company?

These questions may not always appear as obvious red flags in financial statements.

Yet they can tell us a great deal about the quality of governance.
And this is where I believe the conversation around IPO readiness, corporate governance and due diligence needs to go deeper.

Being IPO-ready means you are prepared to enter the capital market.
Being Governance-ready means your Board, leadership, systems and culture are prepared for the accountability that comes with being there.

The real test is not:
“Can we comply?”
It is:
“Are we willing to challenge ourselves before the market does?”

For Merchant Bankers, Promoters, CEOs, CFOs, CXOs and Independent Directors, perhaps this is one of the most important questions to ask before an IPO.

IPO readiness gets a company listed.
Governance readiness helps it stay trusted.

What do you think is the one governance red flag that should make a Board pause before an IPO?

DAY 180/369
 THE 369-DAY LEADERSHIP BLIND SPOT JOURNEY
BLIND SPOT: WHEN LEADERS REWARD LOYALTY MORE THAN TRUTH
Loyalty is valuable.
But there is a dangerous moment when loyalty becomes:
“AGREE WITH ME.”
A team member who always supports the leader may look loyal.

But the person who respectfully says:
“SIR, I THINK WE ARE MAKING A MISTAKE.”

may be demonstrating a much deeper form of loyalty.
Because protecting the leader's ego is not loyalty.

PROTECTING THE MISSION IS.
THE IMPACT
• Honest feedback disappears
• Yes-men rise faster than truth-tellers
• Risks remain hidden
• Leaders become surrounded by agreement
• Organisational decisions slowly become disconnected from reality.

LEADERSHIP MANTRA
DON'T REWARD PEOPLE FOR AGREEING WITH YOU.
REWARD THEM FOR HELPING YOU SEE BETTER.

BREATHCODE — TRUTH SWITCH
INHALE — LISTEN
PAUSE — REFLECT
EXHALE — ACCEPT

Before defending your position, ask:
“WHAT IF THIS PERSON IS RIGHT?”
That single question can protect a leader from a very expensive blind spot.

GOVERNANCE DIAGNOSTIC
👉 “DO PEOPLE AROUND ME TELL ME THE TRUTH—OR WHAT THEY THINK I WANT TO HEAR?”

ACTION TRIGGER
✔ Invite disagreement
✔ Protect respectful dissent
✔ Never punish uncomfortable information
✔ Separate loyalty from agreement
✔ Reward people who identify risks early

IMPLEMENTATION TIP.

In your next review, deliberately ask one trusted person:
“TELL ME WHAT YOU THINK I AM GETTING WRONG.”
Then listen.
DON'T EXPLAIN.
DON'T DEFEND.
JUST LISTEN.

CONCLUSION

A LEADER SURROUNDED BY YES-MEN MAY FEEL POWERFUL.
But a leader surrounded by people who have the courage to speak the truth...
IS PROTECTED.

Because the greatest loyalty is not:
“I AGREE WITH YOU.”

It is:

“I CARE ENOUGH ABOUT THE MISSION TO TELL YOU THE TRUTH.”
— DR. DILIP KUMAR MISHRA

BREATHE WITH AWARENESS.
LEAD WITH PURPOSE.
SERVE WITH HUMILITY.
DELIVER WITH EXCELLENCE.

DAY 181/369THE 369-DAY LEADERSHIP BLIND SPOT JOURNEY
BLIND SPOT .WHEN LEADERS SAY — “WE ARE FAMILY.”

It sounds warm.
It sounds caring.
It sounds like belonging.
But in the corporate world, this sentence can hide one of the BIGGEST LEADERSHIP BLIND SPOTS.

Because an organisation is not a family.
A FAMILY HAS UNCONDITIONAL BONDS.

A COMPANY HAS PROFESSIONAL RESPONSIBILITIES, EXPECTATIONS AND ACCOUNTABILITY.

When leaders repeatedly say:
“WE ARE FAMILY.”
They must be prepared to behave like it—not only when employees are delivering results, but also when people are struggling, disagreeing, asking for fair compensation, seeking growth, or facing difficult circumstances.

Otherwise...
“WE ARE FAMILY” BECOMES A SLOGAN USED TO DEMAND LOYALTY WITHOUT PROVIDING RECIPROCAL CARE.
THE BLIND SPOT
An employee works late.
“WE ARE FAMILY.”
An employee sacrifices personal time.
“WE ARE FAMILY.”

But when the employee asks about:
Salary.
Growth.
Safety.
Workload.
Recognition.
Work-life boundaries.
Suddenly...
THE CONVERSATION BECOMES BUSINESS.
That contradiction destroys trust.
THE IMPACT
• EMOTIONAL LOYALTY IS EXPECTED WITHOUT RECIPROCITY
• PEOPLE FEEL GUILTY FOR SETTING HEALTHY BOUNDARIES
• EXTRA EFFORT BECOMES NORMALISED
• BURNOUT CAN BE MISTAKEN FOR COMMITMENT
• EMPLOYEES STOP BELIEVING LEADERSHIP LANGUAGE.

LEADERSHIP MANTRA
DON'T CALL PEOPLE FAMILY TO GET MORE FROM THEM.
CREATE A CULTURE WHERE PEOPLE FEEL RESPECTED, PROTECTED AND VALUED BECAUSE OF HOW YOU LEAD.

BREATHCODE — RECIPROCITY SWITCH
INHALE — RESPECT
PAUSE — REFLECT
EXHALE — RECIPROCATE
Before saying:
“WE ARE FAMILY.”
Ask:
“WHAT HAVE WE CREATED THAT MAKES OUR PEOPLE ACTUALLY FEEL THEY BELONG?”
GOVERNANCE DIAGNOSTIC
👉 “IF WE STOPPED USING THE WORD ‘FAMILY’, WOULD OUR POLICIES, BEHAVIOUR AND LEADERSHIP STILL MAKE PEOPLE FEEL VALUED?”
That answer reveals the culture.
ACTION TRIGGER
✔ Respect professional boundaries
✔ Pay people fairly and on time
✔ Protect safety and wellbeing
✔ Reward contribution transparently
✔ Allow people to disagree without guilt
✔ Build belonging through behaviour—not slogans

IMPLEMENTATION TIP
The next time you hear:
“WE ARE FAMILY HERE.”
Don't reject it.
Ask a better question:
“WHAT DO WE DO HERE THAT MAKES PEOPLE FEEL THEY BELONG?”
Because culture isn't what leadership says.
CULTURE IS WHAT PEOPLE EXPERIENCE.
CONCLUSION
A COMPANY DOESN'T NEED TO PRETEND TO BE A FAMILY.

It needs to be something equally powerful:
A FAIR, RESPECTFUL, TRUSTWORTHY COMMUNITY OF PEOPLE WORKING TOWARD A SHARED PURPOSE.
Don't use “WE ARE FAMILY” to ask people for sacrifice.
BUILD A CULTURE WHERE PEOPLE CHOOSE TO GIVE THEIR BEST BECAUSE THEY ARE RESPECTED, NOT BECAUSE THEY FEEL OBLIGATED.
— DR. DILIP KUMAR MISHRA

LEAD WITH PURPOSE.
SERVE WITH HUMILITY.

DAY 183/369 BLIND SPOT LEADERSHIP | BREATHCODE

BLIND SPOT : WHEN LEADERS PROTECT THEIR REPUTATION INSTEAD OF THE TRUTH

A leader makes a decision.

The result goes wrong.

Now comes the real leadership test:

ADMIT IT — OR DEFEND IT?

Some leaders continue defending a wrong decision because admitting the mistake may damage their image.

And then a small mistake becomes a bigger problem.

EGO → DEFENSIVENESS → JUSTIFICATION → DELAY → BIGGER DAMAGE

The blind spot isn't making a mistake.

THE BLIND SPOT IS PROTECTING THE IMAGE OF THE LEADER AT THE COST OF THE ORGANISATION.

LEADERSHIP MANTRA

ADMIT FAST.
CORRECT EARLY.
LEARN DEEPLY.

BREATHCODE — TRUTH-OVER-EGO PROTOCOL

INHALE — ACCEPT
PAUSE — RELEASE EGO
EXHALE — CORRECT

Before defending your decision, ask:

“IF I WERE NOT WORRIED ABOUT HOW I LOOK, WHAT WOULD I DO NOW?”

That question can separate EGO FROM LEADERSHIP.

REGULATED LEADERSHIP

UNREGULATED LEADERS PROTECT THEIR IMAGE.

REGULATED LEADERS PROTECT THE MISSION.

A regulated leader can say:

“I GOT IT WRONG.”

Not as weakness.

AS LEADERSHIP STRENGTH.

GOVERNANCE DIAGNOSTIC

Ask:

BLIND SPOT : WHEN LEADERS CONFUSE ACTIVITY WITH PROGRESS
A calendar full of meetings.
Hundreds of emails.
Constant calls.
Reports moving every day.
Teams working late.
The organisation looks BUSY.
But ask one uncomfortable question:
“WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED FORWARD?”
Because ACTIVITY CAN CREATE THE ILLUSION OF PROGRESS.
A team can be extremely busy while the real problem remains untouched.

THE BLIND SPOT
WHEN BUSYNESS BECOMES THE MEASURE OF PERFORMANCE.
The leader sees movement.
But the customer sees no improvement.
The dashboard shows activity.
But the outcome hasn't changed.
BUSY ≠ PRODUCTIVE.
ACTIVITY ≠ IMPACT.

LEADERSHIP MANTRA
DON'T MEASURE HOW MUCH PEOPLE DO.
MEASURE WHAT THEIR WORK CHANGES.

BREATHCODE — OUTCOME SWITCH
INHALE — FOCUS
PAUSE — PRIORITISE
EXHALE — DELIVER

Before starting another task, ask:
“WHAT OUTCOME WILL THIS ACTIVITY CREATE?”

If there is no meaningful answer...
QUESTION THE ACTIVITY.
REGULATED LEADERSHIP

A REGULATED LEADER PROTECTS ATTENTION FOR WHAT MATTERS.
The ability to pause before adding another task...

The feedback women founders get that sounds helpful and quietly isn't


There's a specific kind of feedback women founders hear more than anyone else.
"Just be a bit more likeable in the room."
"Soften how you push back."
"Bring the energy down a little in board meetings."

It's offered gently, usually by someone who thinks they're helping. 
And it usually leads a woman founder to trade sharpness for approval, 
one meeting at a time.

Here's what I've noticed after watching this play out for years.

The advice is rarely wrong about the room. 
It's wrong about what she should do with that information.

Being aware that a room reacts to directness is useful. 
Sanding down your directness to manage that reaction is a different thing entirely.

The founders I've seen build real authority did the first without doing the second. 
They read the room accurately, and then said the hard thing anyway, just more precisely.

Likeability was never the currency that built a company.
Clarity was.

Don't let anyone quietly trade one for the other on your behalf.

Second-guessing whether you're being too direct, too much, too anything? 
Let's talk about what's actually working against you.

Beyond Silos
Well-performing functions do not always create a well-performing organisation.

Some of the most significant execution failures occur even when every department delivers against its own objectives.

The underlying challenge is often weak coordination across interconnected functions.
The warning signs include:
• Limited end-to-end visibility
• Fragmented ownership
• Disconnected workflows
• Inconsistent decision-making

Over time, these gaps result in:
• Avoidable delays
• Repeated exceptions
• Duplicated effort
• Inconsistent stakeholder experiences
• Missed commercial opportunities
• Rising operational complexity

The issue is rarely individual capability.

It is enterprise coordination.

Mature organisations recognise that sustainable execution depends not only on functional excellence but also on how effectively processes, systems, governance, and accountability work together across the enterprise.

Enterprise performance is ultimately determined less by how well individual functions perform and more by how effectively the organisation operates as one integrated system.

Board Question:
What assurance does your board receive that cross-functional coordination is enabling enterprise-wide execution rather than creating hidden operational risk?

post_text:
The Illusion of Control.
The most dangerous governance risk is often the belief that everything is under control.
As organizations grow, governance structures naturally become more sophisticated.
 
Boards receive:
 Dashboards
 Audit reports
 Compliance certifications
 Escalation matrices
 Multiple layers of review

These mechanisms are essential.

But governance rarely weakens first at the policy level.
It weakens through behaviour.

Controls continue to exist institutionally while discipline gradually weakens operationally.

That is what makes the risk difficult to detect.

Reporting can continue to provide confidence even as accountability, review discipline, and control behaviours begin to erode.

Over time, the focus may shift from maintaining disciplined behaviour to maintaining evidence of compliance.

That distinction matters.

Governance maturity is not measured by how well evidence can be reconstructed after the event.

It is measured by whether accountability, effective challenge, and control discipline remain embedded in everyday decision-making—even when no one is watching.

Organizations rarely fail because governance frameworks are absent.
They fail when behaviours weaken while reporting continues to create the illusion that governance remains strong.

Board Question: Beyond dashboards and compliance reports, how does your board gain assurance that disciplined control behaviours remain effective throughout the organization?

Consistency Wins.

Process consistency is often an underappreciated competitive advantage.
Organizations are quick to celebrate speed, crisis management, and heroic effort. 
But long-term institutional credibility is built through consistently reliable execution.
. 
Operational maturity is reflected not in how effectively organizations respond to recurring problems, but in how rarely those problems occur.

As organizations scale, this distinction becomes even more important.
Sustainable operating environments are created by:

• Reducing process variability
• Strengthening execution discipline
• Embedding reliability into the operating model
• Continuously improving process performance

Over time, stakeholders recognize the difference between organizations that rely on individual effort to sustain performance and those where operational consistency has become an institutional capability.

Operational excellence is therefore less about the intensity of effort and more about the reliability of execution.

Competitive advantage is sustained not by occasional operational brilliance, but by an organization's ability to deliver disciplined, predictable, and dependable performance every day.

Board Question: Does your board receive assurance that consistent execution is becoming an institutional capability, or does performance still depend on individual effort and operational heroics?

The Illusion of Control.
The most dangerous governance risk is often the belief that everything is under control.
As organisations grow, governance structures naturally become more sophisticated.

Boards receive:
Dashboards
Audit reports
Compliance certifications
Escalation matrices
Multiple layers of review

These mechanisms are essential.

But governance rarely weakens first at the policy level.
It weakens through behaviour.
Controls continue to exist institutionally while discipline gradually weakens operationally.
That is what makes the risk difficult to detect.

Reporting can continue to provide confidence even as accountability, review discipline, and control behaviours begin to erode.

Over time, the focus may shift from maintaining disciplined behaviour to maintaining evidence of compliance.

That distinction matters.

Governance maturity is not measured by how well evidence can be reconstructed after the event.

It is measured by whether accountability, effective challenge, and control discipline remain embedded in everyday decision-making—even when no one is watching.

Organisations rarely fail because governance frameworks are absent.
They fail when behaviours weaken while reporting continues to create the illusion that governance remains strong.

Board Question: Beyond dashboards and compliance reports, how does your board gain assurance that disciplined control behaviours remain effective throughout the organisation?

Stations are getting glass facades. Passengers can't get safe drinking water

A recent CAG audit found E. coli – an indicator of faecal contamination, in water cooler samples at 8 railway stations across 4 zones, including CSMT, Kalyan, Lonavala, Coimbatore, and Hyderabad. Bacteriological testing hadn't even been conducted at 59 stations across 6 zones. The same audit flagged shortages of over 2,000 water taps and hundreds of toilets and urinals nationwide.

This lands at an odd moment. Indian Railways is pouring thousands of crores into station redevelopment — food courts, escalators, waiting lounges, airport-style facades under schemes like Amrit Bharat. Impressive to look at. But what does modernisation mean if the water cooler at that same "world-class" station can make you sick?

A few questions worth asking:

→ Governance: If testing wasn't done at 59 stations, who was accountable for that gap — and for how long did it go unnoticed?

→ Priorities: Are capital budgets being weighted toward visible, prestige upgrades over unglamorous but essential upkeep — tank cleaning, chlorination, pipeline maintenance?

→ Customer service: Passengers have no easy way to flag or verify water safety at a station. Where's the accountability loop back to them? None of the fixes here are exotic. They just need to be non-negotiable line items — not what's left over after the ribbon-cutting projects are funded.

It would be good to see even a fraction of the redevelopment spend redirected to hygiene and safe drinking water. A station can look modern and still fail passengers on the basics.

₹35,715 Crore Written Off, Zero Names Revealed: A Crisis of Banking Governance and Accountability

Ever noticed how banking rules seem to bend depending on who owes the money?

When a retail customer or small business owner misses an EMI, enforcement is swift—warning letters, credit score hits, public notices in newspapers, and property recovery actions.

Yet, when corporate defaults reach astronomical levels, public sector institutions hide behind privacy exemptions.

The Accountability Gap in Numbers:

A recent RTI disclosure revealed striking facts about Bank of Baroda:
₹35,715 Crore Written Off: Total bad loans written off over six financial years for large accounts owing over ₹100 crore each.

Under 28% Recovered: The bank managed to recover only ₹9,946 crore from these high-value accounts.

₹7,817 Crore Lost to "Haircuts": Absorbed as outright losses during settlements and insolvency proceedings.

Despite these staggering figures involving public money, the bank refused to reveal the names of these corporate defaulters under the RTI Act, invoking privacy and commercial confidence clauses.

Why Governance Matters Here:

Asymmetric Accountability: Small borrowers face public shaming for thousands, while mega-defaulters get institutional anonymity for thousands of crores.

Boardroom Immunity: Executive committees that sanction high-risk, multi-hundred-crore credit facilities rarely face personal accountability or transparent audits when these loans turn sour.

Erosion of Public Trust: When public sector banks use taxpayer-backed capital to absorb massive losses while shielding borrower identities, it fundamentally undermines public faith in banking governance.
Systemic reform requires equal rules for all borrowers, uncompromising transparency, and real executive accountability.

THE INDEPENDENT DIRECTOR’S DESK | FRIDAY BOARDROOM CHALLENGE — WEEK 5

🤫 THE “SILENT DISSENT” TRAP

When your objection disappears from the minutes

Imagine this.

It’s a tense, high-stakes Board meeting.

Management is pushing for approval of a high-value Related Party Transaction (RPT).

You see the red flags:

⚠️ No independent benchmarking study.
⚠️ The counterparty was incorporated only six months ago.
⚠️ The commercial rationale is unclear.

You ask the difficult questions.

You challenge management’s assumptions.

And finally, you clearly voice your objection to the transaction.

The Board proceeds.

Seven days later, the draft minutes arrive in your inbox.

You scroll to the relevant item.

And then you see:

“After due discussion, the Board unanimously resolved to approve the transaction.”

Unanimously.

You immediately call the Company Secretary.

The response?

“Don’t worry, Director. Your concerns were noted during the discussion. But ‘unanimous’ looks better for the consortium of banks and rating agencies.”

🚨 NOW THE REAL BOARDROOM TEST BEGINS.

WHAT WOULD YOU DO?

🅰️ LET IT GO
Your objection was clearly made in the meeting, and you have your own dated notes.

🅱️ REQUEST A SOFT EDIT
Ask the Company Secretary to mention that “certain concerns and clarifications were raised.”

🅲 FORMALLY CHALLENGE THE MINUTES
Write to the Chairperson and Company Secretary, stating clearly that you did not concur with the resolution and requesting that your dissent and material concerns be accurately reflected in the minutes.

🅳 ANOTHER APPROACH?
Tell us exactly how you would protect your position.

⸻

🔎 THE BOARDROOM QUESTION

If the minutes say “unanimous” when you actually dissented—

Is your verbal objection enough?

This is where governance moves beyond what was said in the room to what is preserved in the institutional record.

A conversation can be forgotten.

A verbal objection can be disputed.

But the Board minutes become part of the formal record of the proceedings.

So the real question for an Independent Director is:

“Will the record accurately reflect the position I took?”

And if it doesn’t—

Would you challenge it?

⸻

🧭 YOUR FRIDAY CHALLENGE

A, B, C or D?

But don’t just choose an option.

👇 Tell us what exact step you would take—and why.

Would you insist on your dissent being recorded?

Or is there another way you would protect your position?

⸻

SUNDAY

THE SILENT DISSENT — When a Verbal Objection Isn’t Enough

We will examine:

🔹 What should happen when the minutes don’t accurately reflect a Director’s position
🔹 Why documentation matters when decisions are scrutinised years later

ALGORITHMS OF DHARMA
கெடுவான் கேடு நினைப்பான்
The one who plots another's downfall may unknowingly be writing his own.
I recently went through a strategic roadmap examining possible geopolitical scenarios around 2027.
Energy disruption.
Food insecurity.
Supply-chain vulnerability.
Technology competition.
Information warfare.
Strategic dependency.
But one idea stayed with me:
The most dangerous weapon may not be a missile.
It may be dependency.
A country can have military strength, technology, capital and influence.
But if its food, energy, fertilizer, logistics, technology or information systems depend excessively on someone else...
its strength can become its vulnerability.
And this is where an ancient Tamil wisdom feels remarkably modern:
கெடுவான் கேடு நினைப்பான்
The person who thinks about another's destruction may ultimately create the conditions for his own.
I call this the:
ALGORITHM OF DHARMA
INTENTION → ACTION → CONSEQUENCE → RETURN
Think about it.
Weaponise supply chains → Others build alternatives.
Weaponise scarcity → Others build strategic reserves.
Weaponise trade → Others diversify routes.
Weaponise information → Others build trusted systems.
Create dependency → Others invest in self-reliance.
The strategy creates its own counter-strategy.
That is the feedback loop.
FAO's 2026 assessment highlights how geopolitical shocks to energy and fertilizer markets can transmit into agriculture, food prices and food security.
For India, this makes food security a strategic infrastructure issue, not merely an agricultural one.
But resilience is never a one-time achievement.
It must be continuously designed.
Secure the food.
Secure the storage.
Secure the energy.
Secure the supply chains.
Secure the technology.
Secure the data.
Secure the truth.
And this becomes a boardroom lesson.
Every Board should ask:
What happens if our primary supplier disappears?
What if a critical logistics route is blocked?
What if energy costs suddenly double?
What if our data becomes unavailable?
What if an AI-generated narrative damages our reputation?
What if a geopolitical event thousands of kilometres away disrupts our business?
“We will manage when it happens” is not resilience.
That is reaction.
True resilience means asking uncomfortable questions before the crisis arrives.
The best organisations don't merely predict risk.
They design themselves to survive uncertainty.
Perhaps that is the deeper meaning of Dharma.
Dharma is not merely morality.
Dharma is a feedback system.
You put something into the system.
The system responds.
So perhaps the real question for 2027 is not:
“Who will attack whom?”
It is:
“Who has built enough resilience to absorb the shock?”
Because in a world of scarcity, dependency and subversion:
Resilience is not an option.
It is strategic survival.
கெடுவான் கேடு நினைப்பான்.
Do something to the system.
The system eventually responds.
BUILD RESILIENCE.
ACT ETHICALLY.
THINK LONG TERM.
WIN SUSTAINABLY.

Algorithms of Dharma | Episode 1

The Friendship Recession: When Contacts Multiply and Connections Vanish
We are the most "connected" generation in history — and, by some measures, the loneliest.

American adults reporting zero close friends have quadrupled since 1990. People with 10+ close friends have dropped by a third. Solo dining is up 29% in two years. Stanford now runs an actual course on friendship. 

Harvard's 80-year longitudinal study — one of the longest-running studies on human wellbeing — arrives at a single, uncomfortable conclusion: what predicts a long, healthy, happy life isn't wealth or status. It's the depth of our relationships.

2,000 years before that study existed, Thiruvalluvar had already written the algorithm.
Kural 786 says it plainly: முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று, நெஞ்சத்து அகநக நட்பது நட்பு — "Friendship that only smiles on the face is no friendship; friendship is when the heart smiles within."

That one line separates a contact from a friend. A LinkedIn connection from a relationship. A transaction from a bond.

Somewhere between our growing networks and our shrinking circles, we started optimizing for reach and lost sight of depth. We have more "connections" than any generation before us, and fewer people who would show up at 2 a.m.

For anyone in governance, leadership, or organization-building, there's a quieter lesson here too: trust — the currency every board, team, and institution runs on — is built the same way friendship is. 

Not through visibility, but through consistency. Not through the smiling face in the boardroom, but through the heart that shows up when it's inconvenient.

Loneliness, the research now confirms, carries a health cost comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Yet we still treat friendship as a luxury to schedule "someday."

Call the friend today. Not because an algorithm nudged you — because your ancestors already worked out the formula, and modern science just caught up.

Algorithms of Dharma — "The Four Ministers of the Mind"

A cognitive-coordination app I tried this week told me something I already knew, just in language I hadn't used before.
 
The report — NeuralFusion's Cognitive Coordination Profile — scores four "thinking modes": Clear Logical Thinking, Gut Instinct, Creative Connections, Self-Awareness, and a fifth composite, Staying Steady Under Pressure. Mine came back the way most leaders' probably do: strong on Creative Connections, decent on Gut Instinct and Self-Awareness, and quietly underused on Clear, Logical Thinking — the one that "freezes when the situation has no clear structure."
 
What struck me wasn't the score. It was how old the idea underneath it is.
 
Vedantic psychology mapped this same terrain three thousand years ago, in the concept of the Antahkarana Chatushtaya — the four-fold inner instrument:
 
Manas, the sensing mind — reads a room before the head catches up. (Gut Instinct.) Buddhi, the discriminating intellect — sorts signal from noise and commits to a decision. (Clear, Logical Thinking.) Chitta, the memory-store — pulls threads from everywhere and stitches new patterns from old ones. (Creative Connections.) Ahamkara, the sense of self — the faculty that steps back and asks, "is this actually me deciding, or my conditioning?" (Self-Awareness.)
 
The Gita and the later Vedantic commentators never asked which of the four should dominate. They asked whether the four were working in coordination — whether Buddhi was allowed to discipline Manas, whether Chitta's associative flair was given a Buddhi-shaped container before it reached a decision. A mind where one faculty runs the show and the others go along for the ride isn't a strong mind. It's an uncoordinated one.
 
That's the same finding a modern app just handed me in a donut chart.
 
For those of us in governance and leadership roles, the practical takeaway isn't "go develop your weak mode until it matches your strong one." It's simpler, and it's exactly what a good board does with a talented-but-lopsided founder: build the process that pulls the underused faculty in at the right moment. 

Three facts, written down, before the decision — not because instinct or creativity are wrong, but because Buddhi needs to be invited to the table, not just tolerated when it shows up on its own.
 
Old wisdom, new dashboard. Same instruction either way: coordinate the ministers, don't crown one of them king.

Algorithms of Dharma | Episode 2

Whose truth does the map show you?

Open a digital map in New Delhi, and Jammu & Kashmir is presented as an integral part of India.

Open the same service in Pakistan, and the depiction changes.

View Crimea from different jurisdictions, and you'll notice that some versions reflect Russian control, while others identify it as part of Ukraine.

The satellites are the same. The software is the same. Yet the representation changes depending on where the viewer is.

Most of us accept algorithmic personalization when it recommends a movie, filters our news, or suggests a product.

But what happens when personalization extends to our understanding of geography, sovereignty, or political reality?

Digital platforms often localize maps to comply with national laws and regulatory requirements. 

From a business perspective, that may be understandable.
From a governance perspective, however, it raises a much larger question:

When digital systems present different versions of reality to different audiences, where does objective truth fit?

Our Itihasas remind us that Dharma is not determined by convenience or power. Dharma is that which remains steadfast even when perspectives differ.

Technology, by contrast, increasingly adapts itself to jurisdiction, regulation, and commercial necessity.

Neither approach is inherently wrong.
But leaders should recognize the distinction.

As AI, digital platforms, and intelligent systems become the primary source of knowledge for billions of people, governance can no longer focus only on privacy, cybersecurity, or compliance.

It must also ask:
Who decides what reality a digital system presents?

This is no longer just a geopolitical question.
It is a boardroom question.

The future of digital sovereignty will not be shaped only by governments. It will also be shaped by the policies, algorithms, and governance frameworks designed inside technology companies.

And perhaps the most important governance question of this decade is not whether AI can generate information—
but whether it presents the same reality to everyone.

Algorithms of Dharma — Episode 3 

The Governance Code Hidden in the Rath Yatra

When the CEO "falls sick," the organisation doesn't stop. It restructures.

Every year, millions watch the Puri Jagannath Rath Yatra as a spectacle of scale — three colossal chariots, lakhs of devotees, a festival that gave the English language the word "Juggernaut."

But strip away the crowd and look at the sequence of events, and you find a governance model that any board would recognise.

1. Planned incapacity, not crisis.
Before the Yatra, the deities go through a 15-day "Anasara" — a scheduled withdrawal, no darshan, minimal offerings. This isn't a breakdown. It's a declared, bounded period of reduced capacity — the temple equivalent of succession-readiness. Nothing catches the system off guard because the pause was designed in.

2. Escalation has a protocol — and a cooling-off ritual.
When Mahalakshmi is left behind and finds the gates shut against her, she doesn't sulk — she authorises the breaking of part of the main chariot (Rath Bhanga). Conflict is not suppressed; it is expressed through a sanctioned act with real, visible cost. Then comes de-escalation: a symbolic peace offering (the Agyan Mala), followed by full reconciliation over Rasagola — a gesture, not a resolution memo, but one that actually restores the relationship.

3. Zero waste, by design.
The broken chariots aren't discarded — every plank becomes firewood for the world's largest temple kitchen, which then produces the 56-item Mahaprasad for the very devotees who came to witness the festival. Nothing that served its purpose once is treated as waste; it's redeployed into the next function of the system.

4. The cycle never actually ends.
Within months of one Rath Yatra closing, the search for next year's chariot timber begins on Akshaya Tritiya. There is no "project closed" mentality — only continuous renewal, encoded into the calendar itself.

This is what our Puranas and temple traditions do so well — they don't hand you a rulebook. They hand you a story you retell every year, and the governance logic rides along inside it, generation after generation, without ever needing to be minuted.

Thiruvalluvar said it in one line, two thousand years before "change management" became a slide deck term:
"இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால் என்ன பயத்ததோ நன்று" — loosely: the strength of goodness lies not in reacting to hurt with hurt, but in the discipline of restoring the relationship.

That's not sentiment. That's a functioning conflict-resolution algorithm — 900 years old, still running, still trusted.

What's the oldest ritual in your own family or organisation that, if you looked closely, turns out to be a governance protocol in disguise?

“The sky is not the limit. Your mind is.” — Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam

Sometimes, a quote takes years to reveal its true meaning and sometimes, an entire generation of engineers turns that quote into reality.

For decades, sending an Indian privately developed orbital-class rocket into space would have sounded almost unimaginable.

Rockets belonged to governments.Space demanded enormous institutions, extraordinary capital, sophisticated technology and years of accumulated knowledge.

Then came Vikram-1. India's first privately developed orbital-class rocket represents something much larger than a technological achievement.It represents the stretching of India's imagination.

Think deeply. Before something becomes possible, someone must first have the courage to imagine it while everyone else still considers it impossible.
"That is where every breakthrough begins."

Not with resources.
Not with certainty.
Not even with technology.

It begins with imagination.

But imagination alone cannot launch a rocket.It needs vision to give it direction.
Commitment to survive uncertainty.
Engineering discipline to convert ideas into systems.Courage to accept risk.And above all, perseverance when things refuse to work as planned. Space exploration has repeatedly taught us this lesson.

Some of the world's most successful space programmes endured setbacks and failed launches before succeeding.
Because breakthrough innovation rarely follows:
Idea → Execution → Success.

More often, it follows:
Imagination → Challenge → Failure → Learning → Perseverance → Breakthrough.

vis a vis there is a profound lesson here for boards and senior leadership teams.In boardrooms, we rightly ask:
What can go wrong?
What will it cost?
What is the return?
Has somebody done it before?
These are essential governance questions.

Success of Vikram 1 inspires us to another question:
“What could become possible if we stretched our imagination beyond what appears achievable today?”

Because governance cannot only be about protecting the enterprise from tomorrow's risks.It must also prevent today's thinking from limiting tomorrow's possibilities. Vikram-1 therefore represents more than a rocket.

To me, it represents a mindset:Imagine beyond precedent.Take intelligent risks.
Learn relentlessly.Persevere through uncertainty.And build what others once considered impossible.

Dr. Kalam asked India to dream.
A new generation of Indian engineers is showing us what happens when those dreams are combined with technology, entrepreneurship and relentless execution.

Perhaps the greatest question for every leader is therefore not:
“Is it possible?”
But:“What must we do to make it possible?”
Because every breakthrough was once an impossibility.Every transformation was once merely an idea.And every frontier was once considered beyond our reach.The sky was never the limit.The real limit is how far we are prepared to stretch our imagination.

What made Dr. Kalam extraordinary?
Despite his immense achievements as a scientist, technologist and national leader, he carried himself with extraordinary simplicity, humility and conviction.He made people believe that their potential was greater than their circumstances.

His leadership philosophy was simple:
Dream. Think. Work. Persevere. Serve.
That philosophy has stayed with me throughout my professional journey.

The award was for energy conservation, but for me , its deeper meaning was about responsible stewardship of resources. 

Energy efficiency, sustainability, innovation and operational excellence , my domain areas are not merely technical disciplines. They are ultimately about creating greater value with fewer resources and a stronger sense of responsibility.That thought continues to influence my work.

What can leaders learn from Dr. Kalam?
Dream beyond the obvious.Imagine possibilities before they become realities.
Convert vision into execution.A dream without disciplined action remains an aspiration.Difficulties are often part of the journey towards meaningful achievement.Remain humble despite success.Use knowledge to create impact.Leadership is ultimately about converting knowledge into value for people and society.

Years later, when I look at these photographs, I don't see only an award.I see a standard of leadership.

Think beyond yourself.
Work with integrity.
Create measurable impact.
Persevere when the path becomes difficult.
Use knowledge and position to create value for society.

Dr. Kalam once said:
“Thinking is progress. Non-thinking is stagnation.”

For me, that remains an enduring leadership principle.The greatest tribute to a visionary is not simply remembering his words.It is translating those words into the way we work, lead, innovate and serve.

Receiving an award from Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam remains one of the proudest moments of my professional life.But being inspired by him has been a much longer journey.

An award recognises what you have achieved.A great leader inspires what you are yet capable of achieving.

Forever inspired by Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.

𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆, 𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝘀𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗰𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘀.

I spent three nights straight working with my team to sanitize data, polish graphs, and build bulletproof defenses for a critical quarterly review of our mobile phone business at GTL Limited. 

We walked into that high-stakes room expecting an intense interrogation on our operational numbers.

Instead, the meeting was chaired by 𝗠𝗿 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗼𝗷 𝗧𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗱𝗸𝗮𝗿, the CMD 

He quietly closed the review file without looking at a single graph, leaned forward, and asked one question that completely rewired my understanding of leadership:

"𝒀𝒐𝒖𝒓 𝒅𝒂𝒕𝒂 𝒕𝒆𝒍𝒍𝒔 𝒎𝒆 𝒑𝒓𝒆𝒄𝒊𝒔𝒆𝒍𝒚 𝒘𝒉𝒆𝒓𝒆 𝒚𝒐𝒖’𝒗𝒆 𝒃𝒆𝒆𝒏 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒘𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒘𝒆𝒏𝒕 𝒓𝒊𝒈𝒉𝒕. 𝑵𝒐𝒘 𝒕𝒆𝒍𝒍 𝒎𝒆—𝒘𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒂𝒓𝒆 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒃𝒍𝒊𝒏𝒅 𝒔𝒑𝒐𝒕𝒔 𝒚𝒐𝒖 𝒂𝒓𝒆 𝒍𝒐𝒔𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒔𝒍𝒆𝒆𝒑 𝒐𝒗𝒆𝒓, 𝒕𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒂𝒓𝒆𝒏'𝒕 𝒑𝒓𝒊𝒏𝒕𝒆𝒅 𝒐𝒏 𝒂𝒏𝒚 𝒐𝒇 𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒔𝒆 𝒔𝒍𝒊𝒅𝒆𝒔?

Silence filled the room.

That single moment changed how I looked at corporate governance and business strategy forever. Across my 33 year journey spanning industry leaders like Tata Communications, airtel, Tata Tele Business Services and 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 Jio, the leaders who truly stand out are never the ones who pretend to have zero problems. They are the ones who expose vulnerabilities early and solve them with absolute intellectual honesty.

𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗺𝗲:

- 𝑪𝒐𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒊𝒂𝒏𝒄𝒆 𝒄𝒉𝒆𝒄𝒌𝒔 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒃𝒐𝒙𝒆𝒔, 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒍 𝒈𝒐𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒏𝒂𝒏𝒄𝒆 𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒕𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒔 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒇𝒖𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒆. A tick-box mentality creates institutional blind spots, whereas genuine oversight actively stress-tests assumptions.

- 𝑨 𝒉𝒆𝒂𝒍𝒕𝒉𝒚 𝒃𝒐𝒂𝒓𝒅 𝒏𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒓 𝒊𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒎𝒊𝒅𝒂𝒕𝒆𝒔 𝒎𝒂𝒏𝒂𝒈𝒆𝒎𝒆𝒏𝒕. Instead, it partners with them, offering the empathy and rigor needed to navigate deep structural risks.

- 𝑻𝒉𝒆 𝒃𝒆𝒔𝒕 𝒅𝒆𝒄𝒊𝒔𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒉𝒂𝒑𝒑𝒆𝒏 𝒘𝒉𝒆𝒏 𝒍𝒆𝒂𝒅𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒉𝒊𝒑 𝒇𝒐𝒔𝒕𝒆𝒓𝒔 𝒂 𝒄𝒖𝒍𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒆 𝒘𝒉𝒆𝒓𝒆 𝒃𝒂𝒅 𝒏𝒆𝒘𝒔 𝒕𝒓𝒂𝒗𝒆𝒍𝒔 𝒇𝒂𝒔𝒕𝒆𝒓 𝒕𝒉𝒂𝒏 𝒈𝒐𝒐𝒅 𝒏𝒆𝒘𝒔. If your team is afraid to share failures, you are already flying blind.

That profound lesson is why I pursued my formal IICA Independent Director certification and ESG Strategy credentials—to bring this exact depth of maturity, risk awareness, and strategic foresight to modern boardrooms.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝟮𝟬𝟬𝟮–𝟮𝟬𝟬𝟯. 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹-𝘂𝗽 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝘂𝗹𝘀𝗲-𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘅𝗶𝗲𝘁𝘆, 𝘄𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.
​When I look back at this photograph from the historic launch of Broadband Internet in India by 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗻𝗲𝘁𝗗𝗦𝗟, it brings back an incredible wave of memories. Back then, serving as the Regional Head for Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh—alongside esteemed leaders like Siva Ventures Limited 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗽 CEO Mr. Srinivasan Vaidyanathan and Business Head Mr. Sanjay Pandit, pictured here sitting in the same row as me, alongwith our phenomenal regional teams—we weren't just launching a product. We were introducing an entirely new digital paradigm to the country.
​At the time, the market skepticism was deafening. Critics called wireline broadband a high-risk, capital-heavy gamble in a nation heavily inclined toward voice.
​But we backed conviction over comfort under the leadership of Mr V Srinivasan and Mr Sanjay Pandit
​Through relentless on-ground execution, strategic network expansion, and a clear vision of India's digital destiny, 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗻𝗲𝘁𝗗𝗦𝗟 𝗟𝘁𝗱 went on to become India’s first and most successful wireline broadband company. That landmark success ultimately caught the attention of the Tata Group, leading to its acquisition by 𝗩𝗦𝗡𝗟 (now Tata Communications) and paving the way for the nationwide data revolution that followed.

​𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝟯𝟯 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝘁𝗮𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀:
​Disruption requires foresight, not consensus. The biggest market shifts are always doubted right before they become obvious.
​Infrastructure is built on grit. True transformation demands operational resilience when the roadmap hasn't been written yet.
​Governance meets growth. Scaling a pioneer venture successfully requires an intricate balance of aggressive market capture and strict fiduciary discipline.
​That exact blend of deep operational roots, strategic risk-taking, and formal governance expertise is what I bring to the table today as an IICA-certified Independent Director and Leadership Advisor.
​Whether you are navigating a massive technology pivot, expanding complex digital infrastructure, or seeking board-level oversight that looks beyond the status quo, I am here to help you see around corners.

𝗜𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟲 𝗺𝘆 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲 𝗮 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸𝘀.

"𝘿𝙖𝙙, 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙨𝙥𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙢𝙮 𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙞𝙧𝙚 𝙡𝙞𝙛𝙚 𝙛𝙞𝙭𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙥𝙧𝙤𝙗𝙡𝙚𝙢𝙨 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮𝙤𝙣𝙚 𝙚𝙡𝙨𝙚'𝙨 𝙗𝙪𝙨𝙞𝙣𝙚𝙨𝙨... 𝙝𝙤𝙬 𝙘𝙤𝙢𝙚 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙡𝙤𝙤𝙠 𝙨𝙤 𝙩𝙞𝙧𝙚𝙙 𝙩𝙧𝙮𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙩𝙤 𝙧𝙚𝙡𝙖𝙭 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙮𝙤𝙪𝙧𝙨𝙚𝙡𝙛?"

I was right in the middle of a high-stakes Broadband rollout. My phone was buzzing through dinner, my mind was mapping out network deployment timelines, and I was constantly mentally "absent" even when sitting across from my family.

For over three decades, I had worn my relentless work ethic like a badge of honor. I believed that total dedication meant sacrificing everything else at the altar of professional success.

I looked at my son, and then looked at my wife Madhu, who had quietly carried the weight of my constant absence for years.

The brutal truth hit me: 𝐈 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐨𝐧𝐞

We often spend the first half of our lives building scale, chasing targets, and proving ourselves to the world, assuming that personal presence can be put on a back burner. But life doesn't wait for your career to peak.

That single conversation didn't make me quit my job, but it fundamentally rewired how I lead, live, and prioritize.

𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝟯𝟯 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝘂𝗿𝘀𝘂𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗺𝗲:

- 𝑺𝒖𝒄𝒄𝒆𝒔𝒔 𝒂𝒕 𝒘𝒐𝒓𝒌 𝒊𝒔 𝒆𝒎𝒑𝒕𝒚 𝒊𝒇 𝒚𝒐𝒖 𝒂𝒓𝒆 𝒂 𝒔𝒕𝒓𝒂𝒏𝒈𝒆𝒓 𝒕𝒐 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒑𝒆𝒐𝒑𝒍𝒆 𝒘𝒉𝒐 𝒍𝒐𝒗𝒆 𝒚𝒐𝒖. No title or board seat will ever greet you back with genuine warmth when you walk through your front door.

- 𝑻𝒓𝒖𝒆 𝒃𝒂𝒍𝒂𝒏𝒄𝒆 𝒊𝒔𝒏'𝒕 𝒂 50/50 𝒔𝒑𝒍𝒊𝒕, 𝒊𝒕 𝒊𝒔 𝒂𝒃𝒐𝒖𝒕 𝒂𝒃𝒔𝒐𝒍𝒖𝒕𝒆 𝒑𝒓𝒆𝒔𝒆𝒏𝒄𝒆. When you are at work, be 100% there. When you are home, put the phone down and actually show up.

- 𝑻𝒉𝒆 𝒉𝒂𝒓𝒅𝒆𝒔𝒕 𝒕𝒉𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒇𝒐𝒓 𝒂 𝒅𝒓𝒊𝒗𝒆𝒏 𝒍𝒆𝒂𝒅𝒆𝒓 𝒕𝒐 𝒍𝒆𝒂𝒓𝒏 𝒊𝒔, 𝒗𝒖𝒍𝒏𝒆𝒓𝒂𝒃𝒊𝒍𝒊𝒕𝒚 𝒔𝒕𝒂𝒓𝒕𝒔 𝒂𝒕 𝒉𝒐𝒎𝒆. Admitting to your family that you've missed out takes more courage than presenting a multi-crore strategy to a board.

The Biggest Risk in Rural Banking Is Often Invisible
Most people associate banking risk with NPAs.
But the real risk begins much earlier.
It begins when governance becomes routine instead of proactive.
Many rural financial institutions continue to operate without a dedicated Credit Risk Management Committee or a structured enterprise-wide risk review mechanism.
The consequences are rarely immediate—but they are significant:
• Portfolio concentration silently increases.
• Emerging risks remain undetected.
• Early warning signals are missed.
• Corrective actions come too late.
• Capital and profitability gradually come under pressure.
Good governance rarely makes headlines.
Poor governance almost always does.
Strong institutions don't just manage losses—they anticipate risks before they become losses. That is the essence of sustainable banking.
Key Takeaways
✅ Risk governance should be preventive, not reactive.
✅ Independent risk oversight strengthens credit quality and portfolio resilience.
✅ Regular portfolio reviews and early warning systems help reduce future NPAs.
✅ Governance culture is a strategic asset, not merely a compliance requirement.
✅ A strong Risk Management Committee creates long-term institutional stability.
Questions for Banking Leaders
Does your institution have an effective and independent Credit Risk Management Committee?
How frequently are concentration risk and emerging sectoral risks reviewed?
Are early warning signals discussed at the Board level before they become NPAs?
Is your governance framework creating value—or merely ensuring compliance?
What is the single governance improvement that could most strengthen your institution's risk culture?
Governance is not about avoiding today's problem—it is about preventing tomorrow's crisis.

🚨 More Data Does NOT Automatically Mean Better Lending Decisions

Digital lending is transforming banking, especially rural banking.

But here is the uncomfortable question:
Are we becoming better at making decisions, or simply becoming faster at making data-driven decisions?

Digital lending platforms can generate enormous amounts of data from transactions, devices, digital footprints, behavioural patterns and alternative sources.

But more data does not automatically mean less risk.
Before trusting an automated credit decision, banks need to ask:

🔹 Is the data reliable and relevant?
🔹 Is the data being interpreted correctly?
🔹 Are credit models independently validated?
🔹 Can bias or data gaps distort the decision?
🔹 Who challenges an automated decision when something looks wrong?
🔹 Is there meaningful human oversight?
🔹 Can the decision be explained to the customer and the Board?

🎯 The real issue is not technology. It is governance.
Technology can make lending faster.
Good governance makes lending safer.
The strongest digital lending ecosystem will therefore not be the one with the most data.
It will be the one that combines:
Data + Analytics + Human Judgment + Independent Validation + Strong Governance

💡 Key Takeaways

✅ Data quality matters more than data quantity.
✅ Automated credit decisions still require accountability.
✅ Models must be independently validated and continuously monitored.
✅ Human challenge remains essential for exceptional or high-risk cases.
✅ Boards need visibility into model risk, data risk and technology risk.
✅ In rural banking, technology must improve inclusion without compromising responsible lending.
❓ Over to you
If an AI or automated model rejects a rural borrower, who should have the final authority to challenge that decision?
And another important question:
Should speed of digital lending ever take priority over the quality of credit assessment?
The future of rural banking will not be defined by how much data we collect, but by how responsibly we use it.

🚨 The Loan Usually Warns You Before It Defaults
A stressed account rarely becomes a problem overnight.
The real risk is not missing the warning signal.
It is ignoring it.
Before an account turns into an NPA, look for signals such as:
🔹 Declining cash flows – repayment capacity is weakening
🔹 Delayed repayments – early signs of liquidity stress
🔹 Weak market prices – collateral or business value may be under pressure
🔹 Falling crop output – particularly important in agricultural portfolios
🔹 Irregular account behaviour – unusual transactions can reveal hidden stress
🎯 The Boardroom Question
It is not simply:
“Do we have an Early Warning System?”
The more important questions are:
👉 Are warning signals reaching decision-makers early enough?
👉 How quickly does the institution act after an alert?
👉 Are repeated alerts triggering portfolio-level action?
👉 Do relationship managers understand the why behind the signal?
👉 Are we measuring the speed of response, not just the number of alerts?
💡 Key Takeaways
1. Early warning is valuable only when followed by early action.
2. A single signal may be noise. Multiple signals together can reveal emerging stress.
3. Credit monitoring should move from reactive review to predictive intervention.
4. Strong institutions do not eliminate risk. They identify and respond to it faster.
My Independent Director Perspective
For a Board, one metric deserves greater attention:
⏱️ “How much time passes between the first warning signal and management action?”
Because in credit risk,
Speed of response can determine portfolio quality.

Boards are constituted to provide independent oversight, strategic direction and forward-looking governance—well before a crisis reaches the organisation. Their fundamental responsibility is to safeguard sustainable growth, long-term value creation and the interests of shareholders and stakeholders.

A Board may ask the right question, but at the wrong time. When questioning moves from strategic oversight into operational intervention, the Board risks crossing the line from governance to management. This can dilute independent judgement, undermine management accountability and gradually turn the Boardroom into an extension of the management function.

The Board should remain focused on the “what, why and whether”, while management remains accountable for the “how and when.”

If critical information reaches the Board only after a situation has escalated, it may indicate delayed information flow, weak management reporting or a failure of management controls. That itself is a matter the Board should examine through its oversight lens.

Strong Boards are those that ask the right oversight questions at the right time. Strong Directors are those who ask meaningful, impactful and sometimes uncomfortable questions—firmly, independently, yet with humility.

The objective is not to challenge management for the sake of challenging management, but to ensure that the right risks are surfaced, the right decisions are tested and the organisation remains aligned with its long-term strategic purpose.

The Board's role is not to manage the business, but to ensure that the business is being managed responsibly, transparently and strategically.

Strong governance means asking the right questions, at the right time, for the right reasons—without compromising the independence of the Board or the accountability of management.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐚 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐦 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐫𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥. 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥.

Over two decades of my career were in finance before I was asked to lead India Operations for a multinational electronics manufacturing company.

There was one obvious reality.

𝐈 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐧 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐨𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐈 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐨𝐫 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞.

Initially, I wondered whether that would limit my ability to contribute during operational reviews.

It turned out to be one of my greatest strengths.

Not being adequately equipped to challenge technical details, I naturally gravitated towards first principles. My questions were basic, logical and rooted in common sense.

- Why are we doing it this way?
- What problem are we trying to solve?
- What assumption are we taking for granted?
- If we were starting from scratch today, would we design this process the same way?

Over time, something remarkable happened.

Every member of my leadership team who reported to me told me, in one way or another, that these seemingly simple questions changed how they thought. They would leave the review, rethink the problem, leverage their deep technical expertise and return with significantly better solutions.

The answers were never mine.

They came from the team's technical expertise. My contribution was simply to ask the questions that helped uncover better solutions.

Looking back, I believe not coming from an operations or engineering background helped me avoid one common trap - 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐢𝐚𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐞.

Experts often see complexity because they understand every nuance.

Leaders and boards must also be able to see simplicity.

That is where some of the most powerful questions originate.

This has shaped my perspective on leadership and governance.

Senior leaders and board members do not create value by knowing more than the experts around the table.

They create value by asking questions that expose assumptions, sharpen thinking and bring discussions back to fundamentals.

Sometimes the question that changes the outcome is not the most sophisticated one.

It is the one that makes everyone pause.

Go back to basics.

And think again.

𝐈𝐧 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐨𝐫 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞, 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐚 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐚 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧? 𝐈 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐥𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐬.

post_text:
𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐯𝐞 𝐠𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐢𝐬 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐭. 𝐈 𝐛𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐯𝐞 𝐚𝐯𝐨𝐢𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐢𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐫 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐚𝐦𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠.

One lesson I have learned over the years is this:

𝐆𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐚𝐧 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐞𝐞.

When we avoid difficult conversations, we often tell ourselves we are protecting the relationship.

In reality, we may be protecting our own discomfort.

The person loses an opportunity to improve while believing everything is largely on track.

I have also seen another common mistake - the "feedback sandwich."

A few compliments...
One difficult point...
A few more compliments...

By the end of the conversation, the most important message has disappeared.

The employee walks away feeling good but not knowing what must change.

I experienced this first-hand when I took over the leadership of an operations team.

During my first round of one-on-one feedback discussions with my direct reports, a few of them told me, "This is the first time I am hearing this feedback."

Curious, I later spoke to their previous managers. Each of them said, "I have shared this feedback many times."

I believe both were right from their own perspective.

The feedback had probably been given, but it had been softened, diluted or buried among other messages.

That experience reinforced a lesson I have carried with me ever since:

𝐄𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐛𝐞 𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭.

If someone needs significant improvement, saying, "You can do much better," is unlikely to create meaningful change.
Instead, explain:

What is falling short.
Why it matters.
What success looks like.
How you will support them in getting there.

However, one prerequisite is often overlooked.

𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐠𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐢𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐰𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐦𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐭.

When goals, standards and behaviour are clearly agreed upfront, feedback becomes far less personal. It becomes a discussion about performance against known expectations rather than opinion.

In my experience, many managers struggle with feedback not because they lack courage, but because they never invested enough time in setting clear expectations.

Whether you are leading a team or serving in the boardroom, the principle remains the same:

𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. 𝐇𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡.

What has been your experience with giving or receiving feedback? I would love to hear what has worked well for you.

Over 35 years, I noticed one habit that consistently separated exceptional leaders from the rest. 
 
Surprisingly, it had nothing to do with intelligence, experience, technical expertise - or even charisma.

It was their speed of response.

When I ask someone, "Can you check on this?", the most common response is:
"Sure, I will check."
Later comes the follow-up:
"Oh, I forgot."

Exceptional leaders respond differently.
They act immediately - making the call or sending the message before the moment passes.

There is an old productivity principle:
𝐈𝐟 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐟𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐬, 𝐝𝐨 𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲.

One experience left a lasting impression on me.

I worked closely with the Global COO of a $4–5 billion business. During one of his visits to India to review a new plant project I was leading, I sought his help on an issue involving his global team.

He did not say, "I will look into it" - the response we hear so often.

He acted immediately. Messages went out while we were still in the car, and by the time we reached our destination about an hour later, responses had already started coming in.

It demonstrated respect for people, urgency in execution, and an operating rhythm that inspired everyone around him.

People who respond quickly earn trust because things move forward instead of getting stuck.

Ultimately, speed of response is about reducing the time between awareness and action.

The same principle applies to organisations.

Customers do not compare you with your past.
They compare you with the speed of the market.

Winning organisations sense change early, decide quickly, and execute rapidly.

Sometimes that requires creative destruction - reinventing successful products, processes, and business models before competitors or market forces force the change.

Microsoft and Netflix reinvented themselves.
Kodak and Nokia waited too long.

Which is why the old leadership lesson applies equally to organisations:
𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐠𝐨𝐭 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞.

Boards play a critical role too here.

Beyond reviewing performance, they should continually ask:

• Are we moving at the speed of the market?
• What is slowing our decisions?
• What should we stop, unlearn, or reinvent before the market forces us to?

Good governance is not about slowing decisions.
It is about ensuring the right decisions are made quickly, with the right oversight.

Speed is no longer just an operational metric.

It is a leadership capability.
An organisational capability.
And increasingly, a governance capability.

Because in business, opportunities rarely wait for those who respond tomorrow.

I am curious to hear your perspective.

What is the single biggest obstacle preventing organisations from moving at the speed of the market? Leadership behaviour, organisational processes or governance?

Leadership Reflections | Lessons from Leading a 50:50 Joint Venture
Part 3: Governance Doesn't Slow Growth. It Enables It.

One of the strongest takeaways from discussions on my previous posts was that successful partnerships are built by aligning complementary strengths—not by creating uniformity.
I couldn't agree more.

But alignment does not happen by itself. It has to be institutionalised.
That became one of my biggest leadership lessons while leading IndianOil Total Private Limited, the 50:50 Joint Venture between IndianOil and TotalEnergies.

Both shareholders brought mature governance traditions developed over decades of managing complex businesses.

Our responsibility was not to choose one approach over the other, but to build a governance framework that reflected the strengths of both while serving the long-term interests of the JV.

That philosophy guided several initiatives.
✅ We developed 35+ Policies and SOPs, bringing clarity across functions and reducing dependence on informal practices.
✅ We institutionalised Board Strategy Meets that went well beyond the routine Board agenda.

For a young JV, these became opportunities to pause, reflect on progress, reconcile perspectives, recalibrate priorities and collectively shape the next phase of growth around a shared vision.

We deliberately involved most members of the leadership team. It gave them first-hand exposure to Board-level thinking, deepened their understanding of shareholder expectations and strengthened organisational alignment.
These discussions also helped create the strategic confidence for the Board to support our asset-light manufacturing strategy—the “Strategic Detour” I discussed in Part 2.

By leveraging manufacturing partnerships across India rather than relying solely on owned facilities, the JV rapidly established a pan-India presence while maintaining capital discipline.

Looking back, I see this as more than a business decision.
It demonstrated how Board Governance, Strategy Execution and Capital Allocation can work together to enable bold but disciplined growth.
Governance is at its best when it enables better decisions—not more processes.

When governance, strategy and execution move together, organisations can grow with both speed and discipline.
I remain grateful to the Boards, leaders and teams of IndianOil and TotalEnergies for fostering a governance culture that balanced entrepreneurial ambition with institutional discipline.

Boardroom Reflection
Growth without Governance is Unsustainable.
Good governance doesn't slow organisations down. It gives Boards the confidence to make bold strategic decisions.
Which governance practice has made the biggest difference in your organisation's ability to execute strategy?

Better Questions. Better Boards. Better Decisions.
Sasi Chemmenkottil
Former MD & CEO | Independent Director | Board Advisor

post_text:
Board Succession Should Begin Before a Vacancy Exists

Most organisations begin searching for a director when a vacancy becomes visible.
A director retires. A tenure ends. Someone resigns.
The search begins.
But I believe the strongest Boards begin the conversation much earlier.
Because strategy does not wait for Board vacancies.

AI, cybersecurity, geopolitical uncertainty, energy transition, capital allocation and stakeholder expectations are continuously reshaping the environment in which Boards govern.
The organisation evolves. Its strategy evolves. Its risks evolve.

The question is:
Has the Board's capability evolved with them?
If Board capability is assessed only when a vacancy arises, a strategic capability gap may have existed for years before the search begins.
I have seen the value of building capability ahead of need throughout my executive career.
When we developed a second LPG import jetty, its immediate purpose was resilience. But the capacity also supported future growth and enabled a long-term throughput business.
Years later, while leading an Indo-foreign Joint Venture, we faced another capability challenge.
Building manufacturing facilities across India would have taken years. Instead, we developed an asset-light distributed manufacturing network using existing partners.
Different situations. The same principle:
Build capability before opportunity—or risk—makes it indispensable.
Why should Board capability be different?
Instead of asking:
Who will replace the next retiring director?
Boards could periodically ask:
What capabilities will this organisation need from its Board three to five years from now?
That creates a different succession process:
Strategy → Future Capability → Gap Assessment → Succession Pipeline → Appointment
The appointment becomes the final step. The governance work begins much earlier.
This also changes the potential contribution of Executive Search firms.
Their role can extend beyond responding to vacancies to helping Boards anticipate capability requirements, assess future gaps and develop succession pipelines before appointments become urgent.
Board succession is therefore not an event.
It is a continuous strategic governance discipline.
Perhaps the quality of tomorrow's Board depends on conversations that begin today.

Executive Perspectives on Building Better Boards | Part 3 of 3
Part 1: Define capability before discussing candidates.
Part 2: Build collective capability, not merely individual credentials.
Part 3: Begin Board succession before a vacancy exists.

Question for Board Chairs, NRC members and Executive Search professionals:
Does your Board review future capability requirements continuously—or mainly when a seat is about to become vacant?

Sasi Chemmenkottil
IICA Certified Independent Director | Former MD & CEO
IndianOil Total Private Limited

🚨 Every KPI was improving.
Revenue was growing.

Margins were holding.
Service levels were on target.
The dashboard was reassuring.
But customers were leaving.

That is when a Board needs to ask a different question:
Are we measuring what is easy to report — or what really matters?

Over the years, I have seen how quickly organisations can become comfortable with dashboards.
KPIs bring discipline.
Targets create accountability.
Trends help Boards identify deviations.

But there is a governance risk when the dashboard becomes the reality rather than a representation of reality.
A business can meet its internal targets while customers experience something entirely different.

Delivery may be “on time” — but increasingly inconvenient.
Complaints may be declining — because customers have stopped complaining and started leaving.
Customer satisfaction may remain high — among the customers who stayed.
Revenue may continue growing — while customer concentration quietly increases.

None of the individual KPIs may be wrong.
The problem may be what they fail to reveal collectively.
That is where Board oversight becomes important.
The Board should not manage customer relationships.
But it should understand whether management's metrics are providing an early warning of changes in customer behaviour.

I believe Boards periodically need to look beyond the green dashboard and ask:
→ Which customer metric would worry us before revenue starts declining?
→ Are we seeing customer retention and concentration — not merely sales 
 growth?
→ What are lost customers telling us that existing customers may not?
→ Are complaints being analysed for patterns, rather than simply closed?
→ When did the Board last hear the customer's voice without it being filtered
 through a KPI?

Because by the time customer deterioration appears in the financial statements, the underlying problem may have existed for months.
Good governance does not distrust the dashboard.
It asks what the dashboard may not be showing.

The Boardroom Dilemma
Every KPI is green.
But customers are quietly leaving.
Would you trust the dashboard — or ask management to prove that the business is genuinely getting stronger?


Boardroom Dilemmas™ #08
Real governance decisions from executive experience.
Better Questions. Better Boards. Better Decisions.

Sasi Chemmenkottil
Independent Director | Former MD & CEO | Board Advisor

The Sustainability Report Is Green. But Is the Strategy?
Carbon has crossed a line that many Boards may not have noticed.

It is no longer only a sustainability metric.
In parts of global trade, it now has an explicit price.
The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism is now in its definitive phase. For Q2 2026, the published CBAM certificate price is €75.28 per tonne of CO₂. 

That matters well beyond the sustainability function.
Because when carbon affects product economics, market access and competitiveness, the Board conversation changes.

The questions are no longer only:
“What are our emissions?”
 “Are our disclosures assured?”

They become:
Which products carry the greatest carbon exposure?
What happens to margins if that exposure becomes more expensive?
Which suppliers increase — or reduce — that exposure?
Which CAPEX decisions are changing it?

Indian Boards have made real progress on governance structure and compliance.

But an ISB study of more than 200 directors from BSE 500 companies found an uncomfortable contrast:
98% saw their Boards as compliant.
 Only 17% said their Boards actively shape strategy.
 Only 27% said directors seek information from independent sources. 

That does not mean Indian Boards are “getting sustainability wrong.”
It suggests something more important:
The governance structure may be maturing faster than strategic ownership.

Having spent much of my career in energy businesses, one lesson stays with me:
A transition becomes real when it changes operating and capital decisions — not when it acquires a new reporting label.
The Board does not need to become an expert in carbon accounting.
But it should be able to take the company's five most important products or assets and understand three things:
Carbon exposure.
Commercial consequence.
Capital response.

A sustainability report tells the Board what the company disclosed.
A transition strategy should tell the Board what the company will do differently.

So here is the question I would like Directors, CFOs, CEOs, sustainability leaders and energy professionals to debate:
At the next Board meeting, who should present the company's carbon exposure — the Sustainability Head, the CFO, or both — and what does your answer say about who really owns the transition?

ENERGY TRANSITION & THE BOARD — PART 1

Independent Director | Former MD & CEO | Board Advisor

THE BOARDROOM QUESTION #01
Would Your Board Pass the Performance Test It Applies to Management?

Boards routinely ask management difficult questions.
- Who is underperforming?
- Which capabilities are becoming obsolete?
- Where is accountability weak?
- Who needs development — and when is change necessary?

But there is a more uncomfortable governance question:
Does the Board apply the same performance discipline to itself?

PwC’s 2025 Annual Corporate Directors Survey found that 55% of directors believe at least one fellow director should be replaced.

Among those directors, the leading reason was not attendance or qualifications.
41% said the director did not contribute meaningfully to Board discussions.
Yet 78% of directors also said their Board assessment process does not provide a complete picture of overall Board performance.
That is the paradox.

Boards are expected to hold management accountable.
But Board accountability is different.

There is no CEO above the Board conducting a performance review. Directors must create a culture in which peers are willing to hold peers accountable — without destroying trust, candour or collegiality.

Perhaps a meaningful Board evaluation should ask:
• Are we discussing the issues that matter most to the company’s future?
• Is every director contributing what the business now requires?
• Are we challenging management — and each other — enough?
• Have yesterday’s strengths become tomorrow’s capability gaps?
• What actually changed because of last year’s Board evaluation?

An assessment that produces a report has completed a process.

An assessment that changes behaviour, capability or composition has produced an outcome.

Boards rightly expect accountability from management.
Should they hold themselves to the same standard?

I would value views from directors, CEOs, governance professionals and executive search leaders.

Sasi Chemmenkottil
Independent Director | Former MD & CEO | Board Advisor

Early in my career, I learned a simple but lasting lesson:

When a responsibility is assigned to you,
you become the owner of the issue — not a messenger waiting for someone else to respond.

Delays, dependencies, and silence are part of professional life.

But ownership means taking initiative, following up, removing blockers, and ensuring closure.

Leadership does not always come from authority.
Often, it comes from accountability.

For Independent Directors, this mindset matters deeply:

Oversight requires initiative, not passivity

Responsibility cannot be outsourced

Governance strengthens when ownership is clear

Boards work best when every member treats assigned matters as their own — from first question to final resolution.

Ownership builds trust.
Trust builds effective boards.

The Three-Dot Principle in Governance (⋮)

On almost every webpage, the three dots in the top corner quietly signal one thing:
there’s more here — if you choose to look.

Governance works the same way.

Management presents performance.
Governance ensures depth.

Independent Directors are not expected to micromanage.

They are expected to know when to look beyond what is presented.

In a boardroom, the “three dots” represent: • questions not yet asked
• risks not yet surfaced
• assumptions not yet tested

Good governance does not overload the board with detail.

It ensures that depth, access, and accountability are always available.

When Independent Directors ask the right second-level questions,
they are not delaying decisions —
they are protecting trust.

Boards don’t fail because information was hidden.
They fail because no one clicked the three dots.
