I’m choosing Section 149(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 — one of the most misunderstood yet protective provisions for Independent Directors.

Governance Insight | Section 149(12) — The Shield for Independent Directors

One of the most important protections for Independent Directors is often the least understood.

Section 149(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 clearly states:
An Independent Director is liable only for acts of omission or commission that occur:

With their knowledge, and
With their consent or connivance, or
Where they failed to act diligently

This provision exists for a reason.

Independent Directors are not involved in day-to-day operations.
They do not execute transactions.
They do not manage teams.

Their role is oversight, judgment, and governance.

However, this protection works only when diligence is visible.

For Independent Directors, this means:

Asking questions and recording them
Seeking clarifications and documentation
Ensuring dissent, if any, is minuted
Following up on red flags
Demonstrating active participation

Silence is not neutrality.
Silence can be interpreted as consent.

Section 149(12) is not a blanket immunity 

It is a conditional protection based on conduct.

At SID, we emphasise one principle: Diligence is the strongest legal defence of an Independent Director.

Know the law.
Practice governance.
Protect trust.

When institutions grow, governing bodies manage —

It watches conduct, ethics, conflicts, crisis response, and reputation — quietly, independently, and firmly.

This separation ensures:

Accountability without fear

Independence without isolation

Authority without overreach

Governance runs institutions.
Oversight preserves credibility.

At SID, our focus remains clear: build systems that outlast individuals.

An Independent Director’s Silent Test: Sections 184 & 188

Many believe governance failures happen due to bad intent.

In reality, most begin with undisclosed interests and unexamined related-party comfort.

Sections 184 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 serve as a quiet but powerful reminder:

"Independence is not about intention. It is about disclosure, distance, and documented dissent."

1. Section 184 mandates full and timely disclosure of interests—direct or indirect.

2. Section 188 places strict guardrails around Related Party Transactions (RPTs), even when they appear routine, historical, or “business as usual”.

For Independent Directors, this means:

Silence can be interpreted as consent
Familiarity does not dilute fiduciary duty
Past practice does not legitimise present non-compliance

The real governance risk is not the transaction itself—
 It is the absence of independent scrutiny.

In boardrooms, the most courageous question is often the simplest:

“Have we disclosed everything, and should we step aside?”

This is not compliance theatre.
This is trust preservation.

Independent Directors are not appointed to approve transactions—
they are appointed to protect the institution when transactions feel too comfortable.

If first impressions were enough, board packs would be one slide long.

In reality, governance doesn’t work that way.

In Governance, Assumptions Are a Risk. Due Diligence Is a Duty.

The Companies Act, 2013 does not expect Independent Directors to rely on impressions.

It expects judgment rooted in care, skill, and independent application of mind.

From a board perspective:

Section 166 reminds us that duties are owed to the company—not to narratives

Section 149(6) demands independence of thought, not influence of appearances

Sound governance requires reading complete papers, disclosures, and context—not just executive summaries

A quiet voice in the boardroom may signal prudence.

A simple presentation may conceal strong compliance discipline.

Good directors pause before concluding.

Effective boards decide after deliberation, not perception.

True value reveals itself through patience, inquiry, and documented reasoning.

Respect is a governance habit, not a designation.

Independent Directors don’t earn authority from titles on a visiting card.

They earn credibility from how consistently they treat people—especially when no one is watching.

In boardrooms, it’s easy to respect power.
True leadership is respecting process, people, and perspective—regardless of hierarchy.

An effective Independent Director:

Listens to management without intimidation

Values frontline insights as much as consultant slides

Upholds dignity even during disagreement

Treats every stakeholder as part of the governance ecosystem

Because governance is not about standing above management.

It is about standing with the institution—anchored in fairness, independence, and respect.

At SID, we believe: Respect is not situational.

Ethics are not optional.

Leadership is a daily discipline.

If this thought made you pause, let it guide how you listen, question, and decide—starting at the next board meeting.

DOMS didn’t win by spending more.
They won by thinking better.

For years, stationery brands looked identical.

Same pencils. Same colours. Same thinking.

The Independent Director ecosystem today looks very similar.

Same resumes.
Same certifications.
Same panels.
Same buzzwords around “governance”.

And everyone calls it normal.

At SID, we believe this space is ready for disruption.

Boards don’t need more Independent Directors.

They need board-ready, board-tested, and board-trusted directors.

That means: • Moving beyond paper qualifications to proven judgment

• Shifting from attendance-based learning to decision-based capability
• Replacing comfort-led appointments with competence-led selection
• Making governance measurable, visible, and accountable

Just like DOMS changed the shape, material, and packaging of a pencil,
SID is rethinking the shape of leadership in boardrooms.

You don’t disrupt governance by shouting louder.

You disrupt it by listening better — to boards, to stakeholders, to risk signals.

The future of Independent Directors belongs to those who fix the ignored gaps, not those who polish the same old credentials.

MCA Eases DIN-KYC Burden: Big Relief for Directors

The Ministry of Corporate Affairs has notified a major compliance reform by amending Rule 12A of the Companies (Appointment & Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014.

The most significant change:

📌 KYC filing for Directors (DIR-3 KYC) will now be required once every three years, instead of annually.

What this means for directors:

✅ No more repeated yearly filing

✅ Web-based DIR-3 KYC form continues

✅ Certification only when contact/address details change

✅ Updated information still required event-wise (phone/email/address)

🚫 DIN deactivation provisions remain for non-compliance

The amendment reflects industry feedback and Government’s commitment to simplifying regulatory processes without compromising governance.

A welcome move for independent directors, board professionals and compliance teams!

Why do these enforcement actions signal urgent priorities for all non-bank lenders?

The strategic breakdown of the sustained violations:

→ Prior Approval for Board Restructuring: NBFCs cannot alter more than 30 percent of their board of directors (excluding independent directors) resulting in management change without prior written permission from the RBI. 

→ Mandatory Three-Tier Risk Profiling: Lenders must maintain operational systems to dynamically categorize every borrower into low, medium, and high-risk tiers. 

→ Strict 6-Month Risk Review Cadence: Risk categorization cannot remain static after onboarding; institutions are legally mandated to conduct periodic customer risk reviews at least once every six months. 

→ Real-Time Central KYC Synchronization: Failing to upload customer identity data onto the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR) within prescribed timelines constitutes a direct regulatory breach.

generated_comments.value_add: Regarding More than 9.16 crore enterprises are now registered on the Udyam portal, up from 1.65 crore in April 2023, together employing over 40 crore people. When the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026 cleared the Rajya Sabha on 3 August and the Lok Sabha on 7 August, Parliament rewrote the operating manual for that constituency for the first time in nearly two decades.  I spent twenty years at ICICI Bank before moving to the NBFC side of this business, and that shapes how I read the amendment. In a large bank, an MSME arrives as a file: a balance sheet, a bureau score, a collateral valuation. At a lender like ours, the same enterprise arrives as a person in a tier-three town, often with no audited accounts and no credit history worth the name. The distance between those two versions of the same business is where India’s MSME credit problem has always lived. What matters in the 2026 amendment is not any single clause but the shift in intent. The 2006 Act was built to recognise MSMEs. The 2026 amendment is built to make them resilient.  Cash flow first Ask a small business owner what keeps them awake, and the answer is rarely demand. It is money earned but not yet received. Delayed payments from large buyers, corporate and government alike, have quietly drained the liquidity of otherwise healthy enterprises, forcing them to borrow simply to bridge the gap between work done and payment made.  The amended law sets timelines where the old framework offered none. Mediation must conclude within 90 days, unresolved disputes must move to arbitration within 30 days, and an award must follow within 90 days of pleadings. It also closes the loophole that made winning meaningless: where a challenge to an award drags past six months, courts must release at least half the awarded amount to the supplier in the meantime. A mediated settlement or arbitral award can now be recovered as an arrear of land revenue through the district collector.  Central Public Sector Enterprises must now settle their MSME invoices through the Trade Receivables Discounting System, the RBI-authorised platform that converts unpaid invoices into cash. TReDS volumes have already grown from roughly ₹40,000 crore in 2022-23 to about ₹3.47 lakh crore in 2025-26. For a sector where a delayed receivable can mean a missed payroll, predictability in the payment cycle is not a technicality. It is oxygen.  Room to grow The amendment also moves the power to set investment and turnover thresholds from statute to government notification. On paper this sounds procedural. In practice it removes a trap.  Under legislated ceilings, a successful enterprise could outgrow its category within a year and abruptly lose the benefits that helped it grow: priority-sector credit, procurement preferences, guarantee cover. I have watched promoters hold back an expansion, or split a business across entities, simply to stay under a threshold. That is a policy failure, not an entrepreneurial one. Thresholds can now be recalibrated without waiting for a fresh Act of Parliament, so that scaling up is rewarded rather than penalised. Alongside this, conviction-based penalties give way to graded civil ones, which makes formalisation feel less like a risk.  Visibility is the real constraint Udyam registration becomes permanent, free, voluntary and digital. This may be the provision with the longest tail. The biggest barrier to affordable credit for a small enterprise is not risk. It is invisibility. A business that exists only in cash and informal ledgers is difficult to underwrite, however sound it may be.  Our founder and Managing Director, Jitendra Tanwar, has lived both sides of that sentence. He began at seventeen, selling tractors to farmers in the villages around Jaipur and explaining loan terms to buyers who had never seen a sanction letter. Namdev Finvest today manages over ₹1,829 crore in assets across 137 branches in nine states, serving more than 46,000+ borrowers. The lesson he built the institution around is a simple one: the enterprises the formal system cannot see are not the ones it should avoid. They are the ones nobody has looked at properly.  A verifiable digital identity linked to income-tax and GST records changes that equation. It lets lenders read genuine cash flows, extend collateral-light working capital, and price risk fairly. Formalisation is not an end. It is the on-ramp to capital.  The work that begins now Several provisions become operational only once the rules and notifications follow, and the real test is implementation: how quickly Facilitation Councils clear disputes, how far TReDS spreads beyond the mandated CPSEs, how consistently recovery is enforced on the ground. A well-drafted law delivers value only when it reaches the enterprise in a small town, not merely the well-advised firm in a metro.  That last mile is where the responsibility sits for lenders committed to India’s underserved businesses. Legislation can set the rules of the game; it cannot, on its own, put working capital in the hands of a first-generation entrepreneur. If the 2006 Act taught India to count its small businesses, the 2026 amendment challenges us to back them. Under legislated ceilings, a successful enterprise could outgrow its category within a year and abruptly lose the benefits that helped it grow: priority-sector credit, procurement preferences, guarantee cover. I have watched promoters hold back an expansion, or split a business across entities, simply to stay under a threshold. That is a policy failure, not an entrepreneurial one. Thresholds can now be recalibrated without waiting for a fresh Act of Parliament, so that scaling up is rewarded rather than penalised. Alongside this, conviction-based penalties give way to graded civil ones, which makes formalisation feel less like a risk.  Visibility is the real constraint Udyam registration becomes permanent, free, voluntary and digital. This may be the provision with the longest tail. The biggest barrier to affordable credit for a small enterprise is not risk. It is invisibility. A business that exists only in cash and informal ledgers is difficult to underwrite, however sound it may be.  Our founder and Managing Director, Jitendra Tanwar, has lived both sides of that sentence. He began at seventeen, selling tractors to farmers in the villages around Jaipur and explaining loan terms to buyers who had never seen a sanction letter. Namdev Finvest today manages over ₹1,829 crore in assets across 137 branches in nine states, serving more than 46,000+ borrowers. The lesson he built the institution around is a simple one: the enterprises the formal system cannot see are not the ones it should avoid. They are the ones nobody has looked at properly.  A verifiable digital identity linked to income-tax and GST records changes that equation. It lets lenders read genuine cash flows, extend collateral-light working capital, and price risk fairly. Formalisation is not an end. It is the on-ramp to capital.  The work that begins now Several provisions become operational only once the rules and notifications follow, and the real test is implementation: how quickly Facilitation Councils clear disputes, how far TReDS spreads beyond the mandated CPSEs, how consistently recovery is enforced on the ground. A well-drafted law delivers value only when it reaches the enterprise in a small town, not merely the well-advised firm in a metro.  That last mile is where the responsibility sits for lenders committed to India’s underserved businesses. Legislation can set the rules of the game; it cannot, on its own, put working capital in the hands of a first-generation entrepreneur. If the 2006 Act taught India to count its small businesses, the 2026 amendment challenges us to back them.  Sahil Taneja is Chief Business Officer at Namdev Finvest, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on MSME, rural and green lending across nine states. He spent two decades at ICICI Bank across MSME lending, retail assets, branch banking and priority-sector lending before joining the company.: The core discipline in MSME credit lies in evaluating actual cashflow cycles and surrogate operational telemetry rather than relying strictly on backward-looking audited financials. Maintaining sub-2% delinquency requires proactive monitoring of supply-chain receivables and GST turnover patterns.

Program ini bertujuan memperkukuh usaha dakwah melalui pendekatan yang lebih kreatif, relevan dan dekat dengan masyarakat, selaras dengan perkembangan teknologi serta keperluan semasa.

Inisiatif ini turut menekankan aspek etika media, tanggungjawab sosial serta penggunaan teknologi kecerdasan buatan (AI) secara berhemah dalam dunia penerbitan.
